source.title: Optimal Expert-Attention Allocation in Mixture-of-Experts: A Scalable Law for Dynamic Model Design
source.authors: Jun-Zhuo Li; Pei-Jie Jiang; Chang-Xin Tian; Jia Liu; Zhi-Qiang Zhang; Xu-Ming Hu

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. Some equations and figure content are flattened or garbled, and several plotted values are not numerically reported.
record.tranche_reason: The study refines scaling-law analysis for MoE models by measuring how the optimal internal expert-to-attention compute ratio changes with compute and sparsity, and by comparing alternative loss-scaling formulations. It does not directly test the parameter-versus-token allocation laws in the claim.
record.gate_note: The paper's main experiments vary the expert-to-attention FLOPs ratio in GPT-style MoE models and fit an allocation law. It also fits and validates an extended MoE loss-scaling formula and compares alternative formulas. It does not report a direct test of dense-model parameter/token/compute loss power laws, small-run extrapolation to much larger runs, or the compute-optimal parameter/token split. Cited scaling-law results are not recorded as findings.
record.test_reason: The study fits a Chinchilla-style loss law with N^-α and D^-β terms, plus allocation and sparsity penalty terms, to GPT-style MoE language models. These models span 100M–5B total parameters and up to 1e21 FLOPs. The fit quality bears weakly on V1 in a new (MoE) setting. Its main result, the optimal expert-to-attention FLOPs ratio scaling with compute, matches no version. No result tests extrapolation to much larger runs, the parameter/token compute-optimal split, shape at fixed parameters, other modalities or downstream tasks.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that the optimal expert–attention FLOPs ratio in MoE follows a power law in compute with sparsity-dependent coefficients. They say deviations from it reduce efficiency, and that integrating it into a Chinchilla-style loss law gives a fit that generalises to a held-out sparsity level and guides MoE design under fixed budgets.
record.recipe_differences: The study proposes an allocation-aware scaling framework for GPT-style MoE models, including an expert-to-attention FLOPs ratio and sparsity terms; it does not reproduce the original dense-model scaling experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: The optimal-ratio scaling coefficients depend on sparsity. The paper also reports different fit quality across loss-scaling formulations and says alternative efficiency-loss forms fit less well.

fits_no_version.finding: At fixed per-token compute, the loss-minimising expert-to-attention FLOPs ratio r* rises as a power of total compute. Its coefficient and exponent depend on sparsity as power laws: αr=6.7e-5(1−S)^-1.23, βr=0.24(1−S)^0.21.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In MoE LMs, the compute-optimal internal expert/attention compute allocation grows as a sparsity-dependent power of compute.

fits_no_version.finding: Published MoE loss laws fit this study's losses poorly: Wang et al. fails at all scales, and Abnar et al. errs on small models. The study's own formula fits better.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: MoE loss-scaling formulas disagree, and formulas that ignore activation fraction or internal allocation misfit losses.

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: Most reported fit comparisons are qualitative, with no numerical prediction-error metric or uncertainty estimates. Several plotted values are not tabulated. The study's main allocation result concerns expert-versus-attention compute in MoE models rather than the parameter-versus-token allocation in the claim.
record.rows_left_out: No otherwise eligible reported results were left out.

untested.parts: Separate power laws in N, D or C with the other quantities non-bottlenecking; quantitative fit error; dense models.
All of it. Validation holds out a sparsity level, not larger runs.
All of it. No loss-minimising N and D vs compute are reported.
All of it. Depth and heads are held fixed; the r sweep is at fixed per-token compute, not fixed parameter count.
All of it (text LM pretraining only).
Effect of parameter counting, schedule, data or fitting method on the exponents or the N/D split. There are no rows bearing on it.

missing.what: Fitted coefficients of the extended law. The N exponent is α=0.6288 and the D exponent is β=0.0453, far from dense-model values; τ=13.74, a=15.12, b=18.62.
The r* selection rule: when r* falls as compute rises, a suboptimal point within 0.001 loss is substituted. This can enforce the monotonic trend.

record.verdict_notes: Sparsity labels are inconsistent across the paper: Figure 6 says 93.75% for 65 experts, but the setup gives 95.38%; the Figure 5(b) caption misattributes the formula to Wang et al. The r* selection rule biases toward monotonic growth. The D exponent of 0.045 in Table 1 is unusually small, but the extra terms make it non-comparable to dense laws. The record's V7 links were reassigned because the rows concern the allocation ratio or the study's own-method comparisons.

versions.untested_parts: The study tests an extended loss-scaling formula for MoE models, not separate power-law loss curves in parameters, tokens, and compute with the other quantities held non-bottlenecking; it does not establish the claimed several-orders-of-magnitude range.
No reported test fits loss laws on small runs and evaluates loss prediction on runs orders of magnitude larger.
The study optimizes the ratio of expert to attention FLOPs, not the loss-minimizing parameter count and training-token count as functions of total compute.
No comparison isolates the effects of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
The study is restricted to autoregressive language modeling and does not test other modalities or training regimes.

The study tests dependence on MoE sparsity and scaling-formula choice, but does not systematically vary parameter counting, training schedule, data, or fitting method to assess their effects on the parameter-token compute-optimal split.

relationships.condition: GPT-style MoE LMs, 100M–5B total params, up to 1e21 FLOPs, fitted with an extended N^-α + D^-β law plus allocation terms
relationships.reason: The authors report strong agreement of the fitted law on fit data and on held-out sparsity, and close trajectory alignment (R7, R8, R9). The evidence is qualitative only and comes from a joint multi-term fit.
relationships.display_finding: The fitted law agrees closely with fitting data and held-out sparsity settings, with aligned loss trajectories.
